film.title: The Thirteenth Chair
film.synopsis_safe: A visiting medium conducts a séance at a gathering in Calcutta, hoping to shed light on an unsolved murder. When the evening takes another violent turn, Inspector Delzante must question the guests and reconstruct what they believe they witnessed.

reveals.title: Inspector Delzante discovers rehearsed séance notes revealing Wales and La Grange's secret script
reveals.safe_preview: Complete this film before opening its retrospective analysis.
reveals.revealed_fact: Delzante produces written notes showing that Wales and Madame La Grange had rehearsed the seance script in advance. He explains Wales believed a woman killed Spencer Lee and wanted to trick her into confessing.

reveals.title: Madame La Grange confesses to Inspector Delzante that Helen O'Neill is her biological daughter
reveals.safe_preview: Complete this film before opening its retrospective analysis.
reveals.revealed_fact: To prevent the search, Madame La Grange admits that Helen O'Neill is her biological child and that seeing her unexpectedly made her panic and attempt to protect her.

reveals.title: Miss Eastwood hysterically breaks down and confesses to murdering both Wales and Spencer Lee
reveals.safe_preview: Complete this film before opening its retrospective analysis.
reveals.revealed_fact: Inspector Delzante states that Miss Eastwood killed Wales to prevent him from receiving Lee's message, and killed Spencer Lee earlier. Miss Eastwood sobbing admits that she had to do it.

proofs.title: The Fake Séance Conspiracy Between Edward Wales and Madame La Grange
proofs.summary: Delzante's discovery of prepared séance notes changes how Wales's apparently adversarial relationship with La Grange can be read. The later disclosure connects the two participants through a planned performance intended to elicit information about the murder. Wales's introduction of the medium and insistence on controlled conditions can now appear to support that performance rather than simply test it from outside. The written preparation is the recorded evidence; treating every stern remark or locked door as a calculated part of the trap is an interpretation. Those precautions could serve practical purposes as well. The notes also do not establish Wales's private beliefs about spiritualism. The strongest retrospective connection is that apparently independent roles were coordinated in advance, making the earlier public interaction less straightforward than it first appeared.

proofs.blind_explanation: On a first viewing, Edward Wales appears to be an uncompromising skeptic demanding strict scientific test conditions to evaluate a visiting medium. When Madame La Grange promises an honest séance without monetary compensation (ttc-archive-1929-c01-e11), Wales orders all doors locked (ttc-archive-1929-c02-e04) and introduces her to the room as an independent investigator (ttc-archive-1929-c01-e08). Viewers reasonably infer that Wales is conducting an objective, adversarial trial of La Grange's spiritualist claims to determine whether genuine supernatural phenomena or fraudulent tricks will occur under strict dark-room conditions.
proofs.reveal_explanation: Delzante's discovery of prepared séance notes changes how Wales's apparently adversarial relationship with La Grange can be read. The later disclosure connects the two participants through a planned performance intended to elicit information about the murder. Wales's introduction of the medium and insistence on controlled conditions can now appear to support that performance rather than simply test it from outside. The written preparation is the recorded evidence; treating every stern remark or locked door as a calculated part of the trap is an interpretation. Those precautions could serve practical purposes as well. The notes also do not establish Wales's private beliefs about spiritualism. The strongest retrospective connection is that apparently independent roles were coordinated in advance, making the earlier public interaction less straightforward than it first appeared.
alternative_explanations: Locked doors and controlled conditions can have practical investigative purposes alongside theatrical ones.
Prepared notes do not by themselves establish either participant's private beliefs about spiritualism.

proofs.title: Madame La Grange's Tactical Silence to Protect Her Secret Daughter
proofs.summary: La Grange's declaration that Helen O'Neill is her daughter supplies a personal connection missing from the earlier scenes. Helen's request that she remain and their emotional embrace now carry the possibility of recognition and attachment, rather than merely hospitality toward a visitor. The disclosure also supports a protective reading of La Grange's hesitation during the séance: naming a suspect could endanger someone to whom she is closely connected. This is a retrospective interpretation of the recorded behavior, not direct evidence of every thought behind it. The observed admission establishes the relationship; the earlier hesitation does not independently prove a calculated refusal or exclude shock and distress. The meaningful change is that apparent professional failure can be understood in the light of a concealed family bond. Whether she feared actual guilt, a false accusation, or the consequences of exposure is not settled by these observations alone.

proofs.blind_explanation: When Helen begs Madame La Grange to stay for the séance (ttc-archive-1929-c02-e03), viewers naturally assume the fortune teller is simply moved by a polite request from a sympathetic young lady. Their subsequent emotional embrace in the adjoining room (ttc-archive-1929-c02-e08) seems like a poignant moment of maternal warmth from a lonely woman toward a kind hostess's secretary. Later, when La Grange stammers vaguely during the dark trance without delivering the promised suspect's name (ttc-archive-1929-c03-e05), it appears that the medium's trickery faltered or that genuine trance exhaustion interrupted the spiritual communication.
proofs.reveal_explanation: La Grange's declaration that Helen O'Neill is her daughter supplies a personal connection missing from the earlier scenes. Helen's request that she remain and their emotional embrace now carry the possibility of recognition and attachment, rather than merely hospitality toward a visitor. The disclosure also supports a protective reading of La Grange's hesitation during the séance: naming a suspect could endanger someone to whom she is closely connected. This is a retrospective interpretation of the recorded behavior, not direct evidence of every thought behind it. The observed admission establishes the relationship; the earlier hesitation does not independently prove a calculated refusal or exclude shock and distress. The meaningful change is that apparent professional failure can be understood in the light of a concealed family bond. Whether she feared actual guilt, a false accusation, or the consequences of exposure is not settled by these observations alone.
alternative_explanations: The hesitation could reflect emotional shock rather than a fully planned protective tactic.
Concern for a daughter does not establish a belief that the daughter committed a crime.

proofs.title: Miss Eastwood's Panic and Guilt as the Double Murderer
proofs.summary: Eastwood's later confession connects the earlier killing of Spencer Lee with Wales's death during the séance. It also gives her scream during the reconstruction a new possible meaning: fear of exposure rather than only fear of a frightening room. The sequence links Wales's demand for a name, the disturbance in darkness, and the later breakdown into a retrospective account of silencing someone who could reveal the crime. The admission is the recorded basis for identifying Eastwood; an observer cannot reconstruct her exact movements from the blacked-out images. Likewise, the scream alone would not prove guilt without the later confession. The interpretation should preserve that distinction between a character's admission, the detective's reconstruction, and events that the camera does not visibly show.

proofs.blind_explanation: Wales demands the killer's name during the first séance, and a disturbance follows in darkness. The blackout prevents the viewer from identifying an attacker by sight. Delzante's later comment about four gentlemen hesitating to lift the body adds suspicion, but hesitation alone neither identifies the killer nor establishes the attacker's gender. During the reconstructed séance, Eastwood's scream can initially be understood as fear of returning to the conditions of the killing. Darkness, an unsettling performance, and the memory of the earlier death provide reasons for an innocent guest to be distressed. Before the later admission, the distinction between ordinary terror and fear of exposure remains unresolved.
proofs.reveal_explanation: Eastwood's later confession connects the earlier killing of Spencer Lee with Wales's death during the séance. It also gives her scream during the reconstruction a new possible meaning: fear of exposure rather than only fear of a frightening room. The sequence links Wales's demand for a name, the disturbance in darkness, and the later breakdown into a retrospective account of silencing someone who could reveal the crime. The admission is the recorded basis for identifying Eastwood; an observer cannot reconstruct her exact movements from the blacked-out images. Likewise, the scream alone would not prove guilt without the later confession. The interpretation should preserve that distinction between a character's admission, the detective's reconstruction, and events that the camera does not visibly show.
alternative_explanations: A scream in a recreated murder scene can express ordinary fear; its significance depends on the later admission.
The blackout leaves the exact physical movements unobserved even after the narrative identifies the killer.
